big_idea: Numbers split into tens and ones. Different splits help with different problems.
learning_intention: We are learning to compose and decompose numbers to 50 in many ways using tens, ones, and partner pairs.
student_learning_goal: I can compose and decompose any number to 50 using tens, ones, and partner pairs in different ways.
success_criteria: I can show any number 0-50 as tens and ones.
I can find at least two different ways to break a number apart.
I can put two parts back together to compose a target number.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart 'Break Apart 32' showing 4 different decompositions side-by-side

OPTIONAL: Lila and Otto — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Whole-class set of base-ten rods (visible to all)
Lesson 3 formative tracker (Decompositions) — provided in assessment_suite stage
Mid-unit Numerals 0-50 Check-In worksheet (provided in formative_reflection stage)

minds_on.hook: Otto has 32 marbles. He wants to put them in 2 jars. How many ways can he split them? Scoot brings out a rod stack: 'Make 50 your way — Scoot's curious!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Hold up Otto and 3 base-ten rods + 2 ones (= 32).

'Friends — Otto has 32 marbles. He wants to share them between two jars. But he wants to know — how many DIFFERENT ways can he split them?' Pause. Take responses. Most children will offer one or two splits.

Demonstrate: 'Watch.' Place all 32 base-ten pieces into Jar A. 'Way 1: 32 in Jar A, 0 in Jar B.' Move 1 ten-rod across. 'Way 2: 22 in Jar A, 10 in Jar B.' Move another ten. 'Way 3: 12 + 20.' Continue: '2 + 30. 32 + 0 reversed = 0 + 32.'

Pause and reframe: 'Each of these is a way to BREAK 32 APART. We call this DECOMPOSING. The opposite — putting two parts together to make 32 — is COMPOSING. Today we are going to do BOTH. We'll find all the partner pairs of 32, and then we'll use that flexibility to solve problems faster.'

Write on the chart: '32 = 30 + 2'. 'Now — what's another way? Anyone?' Take responses. Add: '32 = 25 + 7' (ten + ten + ten - 3 + 7? No, harder.) '32 = 16 + 16'. The key insight: ten-and-ones is just ONE way; many partner pairs work.
student_actions: Listen as Otto's marbles are split.
Predict the next split before the teacher demonstrates.
Help count each split aloud as a class.

steps.instruction: Whole group: lead a structured decomposition of 32. The class fills the chart together with 4-5 different partner pairs (10+22, 20+12, 5+27, 16+16, 25+7, 30+2). Read each aloud.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Let's fill this chart together. We've already got 30 + 2. What's another partner pair that adds to 32? Hmm — what if I take some ones from the 2 and add them to the 30?' Take responses. Discuss what works and what doesn't (any pair that adds to 32 works).

steps.instruction: Introduce the Make-the-Number game. Each pair gets base-ten rods (M3) and a target number card (e.g. 27, 35, 42). Player A builds the target with rods. Player B says one decomposition: '20 + 7' or '10 + 17' or '15 + 12'. Switch.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You and your partner are going to play Make-the-Number. Player A — build the target number with base-ten rods. Player B — say one way to break it apart. Then switch.' Demonstrate with one pair.

steps.instruction: Stretch round: each pair gets a target ≥ 30 and is challenged to find FOUR different decompositions. Use the Decomposition Worksheet sheet to record them.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Now you'll find FOUR ways. Use your worksheet to record each one. The catch — they all have to be DIFFERENT.' Walk around. Watch for pairs who keep using ten-and-ones decompositions; nudge them toward partner-pair decomp (e.g. 17 + 13 instead of 30 + 0).

steps.instruction: Mid-unit Numerals 0-50 Check-In: hand out the 4-prompt worksheet. Children complete it independently while the teacher circulates with the formative tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You're going to do a quick check on your own — four prompts. Take your time. Use base-ten rods if you need to.' Walk around. For each child, record on the tracker whether they (a) decomposed in tens+ones, (b) found a non-tens+ones partner pair, (c) recomposed correctly, (d) wrote the equation.

steps.instruction: Class debrief and chart-build. Bring children back. Display the Decomposition Worksheet with the most creative decompositions. Discuss which decompositions help with which problems.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Look at all the ways we broke apart 32. Which would be FASTEST for a problem like 32 - 12?' Lead them to '20 + 12' (subtract the 12 directly, leaves 20). 'Which would be fastest for adding 32 + 8?' Lead them to '30 + 2' (add 8 to the 2 = 10, then 30 + 10 = 40). The point: different decompositions serve different problems.

differentiation.for_emerging: These children focus on tens-and-ones decomposition only. Target numbers stay in 10-20 range. The goal is to see that 17 = 10 + 7 and to recompose. Multi-decomposition stretch comes once that's solid.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch cards: 'Decompose 47 in FIVE different ways' or 'What's a decomposition of 50 that DOESN'T use 25 + 25?' Stays inside B1.2 with stretch into Grade 2 territory.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a base-ten rod reference card showing the structure of each rod. Allow physical demonstration over verbal explanation. Pair with a strong-decomposer peer.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Stand-up version: pairs use a giant ten-rod (printed letter-size) and giant ones. The act of moving the rods between jars (yarn circles on the floor) physicalises the decomposition.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Can the child find tens-and-ones decomposition? Can they find at least one partner pair that ISN'T tens-and-ones (e.g. 17 + 5 instead of 20 + 2 for 22)? Can they recompose? The non-tens-and-ones partner pair is the B1.2 mastery signal — it shows flexibility.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the tracker per child as you observe. The 'finds non-tens-ones partner pair' column captures B1.2 mastery.
tracker_columns: Recomposes two parts back to target

discussion_prompts: What was your favourite decomposition you found today?
When is breaking a number into tens-and-ones useful? When isn't it?
If I had 47 and wanted to add 3, how would I decompose? Why?
Can you tell me ONE thing in your everyday life that you could decompose? (e.g. 24 cookies in 4 boxes, 32 minutes split between two activities.)
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child whispers to a partner: 'I broke 35 into ___ + ___.' Partner says back what they would do differently. Then each pair packs up base-ten rods, and the class lines up at the door. Scoot scoots to the next group: 'Make-and-break is BRAIN-power!'

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Decompositions tracker for B1.2 (per-child per-decomp). Mid-unit Numerals 0-50 Check-In worksheet score.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: B1.2 says 'compose and decompose using a variety of tools and strategies' — the keyword is VARIETY. Single-strategy decomposition (always tens-and-ones) misses the point. The tracker's 'non-tens-ones partner pair' column is the mastery signal. Children who can ONLY do tens-and-ones are emerging.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child does only tens-and-ones — repairing single-strategy decomposition for B1.2
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: The most common Grade-1 trap on B1.2 is the child who learns 'every number splits into tens and ones' and treats THAT as the whole answer. They write 32 = 30 + 2 every time. The lesson asks for four different decompositions, and they freeze. This isn't a strategy failure — it's a 'the textbook said so' rigidity. The repair is to physicalise the strategies with base-ten rods so the child SEES that other splits also work.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Step 3 (find 4 different decompositions of 32). The child has written '30 + 2' on their worksheet and stopped. They're staring at the page. The teacher walks up.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'You've got 30 + 2. That's a decomposition. Now I want THREE MORE. Different ones.' The child looks confused. 'How can you have more than one?'

Pick up base-ten rods. Build 32 (3 rods + 2 ones). 'Watch what I do.' Take 5 ones from the pile and add them to the rods, then take 5 from the rods... no, simpler: 'Move ONE rod over here.' Move a rod to the left side. 'How many here?' (10.) 'How many there?' (22 — 2 rods + 2 ones.) 'So 32 = 10 + 22. That's another decomposition.' Write it.

'Now move a rod back, but take it apart into ones first. So this side has 2 rods and 5 ones (= 25), other side has 1 rod and... 7? Yes — 25 + 7.' Write it.

'See — every time I move some pieces around, I get a NEW decomposition. The total is still 32. I just split it differently.' Go through 2-3 more: '15 + 17' (1 rod + 5 ones, 1 rod + 7 ones), '16 + 16', '20 + 12'.

Let the child try one. They'll usually break the rigidity at this point. If they still default to 30+2, send them back to the rods for 1:1 with you for the next 5 minutes. The decomposition flexibility comes from physical play, not verbal instruction.

The long-term recovery move: every Friday, have a 'decomposition challenge' where the class gives ONE target number (chosen by a child) and the class collectively finds as many decompositions as possible. The flexibility is built through repeated play, not a single lesson.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Writes only 30 + 2 and stops. Hasn't yet seen that decomposition has multiple answers. Most common Grade-1 starting point.
(Mid) After the rod-moving demo, can find a few more decompositions but defaults to 'easy' splits (10+22, 20+12). Misses creative pairs (17 + 15).
(Strong) Finds 4+ decompositions independently, including non-tens splits. Uses partner-pair logic (e.g. 'I bet 25+7 works because they look like a partner pair to me').
(Stretched) Volunteers: 'I bet I could find 10 different decompositions if I had more time. Each one moves stuff around differently.' Has internalised that decomposition has many valid answers.
common_misconceptions: Decomposition has one answer. (Most common Grade-1 trap. Repair: show the rod-moving demo on the carpet so the child SEES that any split totals the same.)
Decomposition only works in tens and ones. (True for one strategy, but partner pairs like 17 + 15 = 32 also work. Repair: encourage non-tens splits in Step 3.)
The bigger part of a decomposition is always 'right'. (Some children think decomposition means 'split into mostly-the-target plus a little'. Repair: show 16 + 16 as an even split — equally valid.)
recovery_moves: Always physicalise the decomposition with base-ten rods. The act of moving rods between two sides shows that the total stays the same.
Use both even-split (16 + 16) and lopsided-split (5 + 27) as model examples. Children who only see lopsided splits miss that decomposition can be balanced too.

Connect to addition strategies. '20 + 12' is the easy way to compute 12 + 8 + 12 (decomposing 12 as 10 + 2 first, then adding 10 to 12). The decomposition serves the computation, not just the worksheet.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of B1.2 — composing and decomposing numbers to 50 in multiple ways.

parts_outline.task: Three target numbers (15, 27, 42). For each, the child writes ONE tens-and-ones decomposition and ONE non-tens decomposition.
Two compose tasks. Task A: '___ + ___ = 32'. Task B: '___ + ___ = 47'. The child fills in three different partner pairs for each (six pairs total).
Open prompt: 'Pick a number between 25 and 50. Find AS MANY decompositions as you can.' The child writes their target and lists at least 4.
